newsitem.title: TANZANIA: African leaders, Christopher in Burundi talks.
newsitem.headline: African leaders, Christopher in Burundi talks.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher on Friday opened talks with East African leaders aimed at boosting peace efforts in Burundi.
Christopher arrived in Arusha, northern Tanzania from Ethiopia and immediately went into a meeting with host President Benjamin Mkapa.
He was later to lunch with Mkapa, Kenyan President Daniel Arap Moi and Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni and to hold talks with former Tanzanian President Julius Nyerere.
The African leaders are involved in trying to end a civil war in Burundi that has taken 150,000 lives since October 1993 and encourage negotiations toward a political settlement there.
Regional leaders imposed sanctions on Burundi after a July 25 coup by the Tutu-led military ousted an interim power-sharing government with the main Hutu party.

The leaders are to hold a summit here on Saturday to assess the effect of regional sanctions and consider next steps. U.S. officials said the sanctions have had more political than economic effect because of "substantial leakage".
Although the Burundi war has worsened and the main Tutu and Hutu faction leaders have yet to agree on peace talks, a senior U.S. official told reporters accompanying Christopher:
"I think there is considerablely more hope that the issue of Burundi can be resolved without national suicide than there was back in May."
Another U.S. official called Burundi "one of the most intractable conflicts I've ever seen". But the determination of regional leaders to work together was positive, he said.
The officials said Christopher was kept abreast of the explosive situation in eastern Zaire, where the government accuses Rwanda's Tutsi army of backing ethnic Tutsis in destabilising the region.
Rwanda denies the charge and instead accuses Zaire of backing the country's 40,000-strong former Hutu army ousted in 1994 after the genocide killings of a million Tutsis and moderate Hutus.
"The American strategy is to defuse the tension between Rwanda and Zaire while concentrating on a quick-fix solution to the Burundi crisis," a diplomat said.
But officials said the absence of Zairean strongman Mobutu Sese Seko from his vast African country because of illness had added a twist to the Rwanda-Zaire conflict.

African diplomats said regional East African leaders would be joined later on Friday by counterparts from Rwanda, Ethiopia, Zambia, Zairean Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo and Organisation of African Unity (OAU) Secretary-General Salim Ahmed Salim to push for U.S. support for sanctions imposed against Burundi.

The embargo imposed in July after Burundi strongman Pierre Buyoya overthrew the Hutu government of president Sylvestre Ntibantunganya has received little or no support at all from influential western powers.
A committee of ambassadors appointed by the heads of state to monitor sanctions met for two days from Monday but insiders said it was sharply divided on the next course of action.

Diplomats said Tanzania, the driving force behind the economic and transport embargo on Burundi, wanted the package tightened to force Buyoya to make drastic concessions to Hutus fighting his Tutsi army.
But other countries feel Buyoya should be given an olive branch to thwart the likelihood of hardline commanders in his army pushing him out.
Foreign ministers meet on Friday evening to hammer out a united stand to be presented to the heads of state on Saturday.
